You master Spanish’s two words for “for”: POR (cause, route, exchange) and PARA (purpose, destination, deadline).
for (purpose), towards, in order to, by (deadline)
I’m learning Spanish to work in Spain.
To use PARA for purpose, recipient, direction and deadline.
To use POR for cause, place you pass through, exchange, means and period.
To learn the set expressions with POR: por eso, por fin, por supuesto…
To say “in order to” (para + infinitive) and “because of” (por).
To never again confuse “gracias por” with “para”.
Kenji is organising a charity lunch at his restaurant. Mihai and Ana come to help.
Thanks for coming! Today we’re cooking for a hundred homeless people.
Of course. What shall we do? We’re here to help.
Mihai, you chop the vegetables for the soup. Ana, could you go and get the bread? The bakery is just round here.
Sure. When do you need it by?
By twelve. We open at half past twelve.
Kenji, why are you organising this? It’s a lot of work.
For my grandmother. She did the same thing in Osaka every Sunday. I do it for her.
How lovely! (Later) I’ve got the bread! I paid ten euros for twenty baguettes.
Perfect. For your first time, you’re excellent volunteers.
Hey, why don’t we do it once a month?
Seriously? That would be brilliant! That’s why I love you so much.
For me, this is better than any luxury restaurant.
(At half past twelve) At last! People are coming. Come on, team!
Por: one short syllable. Para: PA-ra, stressed on the first. In fast speech, “para” becomes “pa”: “pa’ ti”, “pa’ casa” (informal).
The final r in “por” is short, a single tap: “por eso” = “po-reso”.
1. PARA: where to and what for
Think of PARA as an arrow POINTING FORWARD, towards a target.
Para ser niño, habla muy bien.
For a child, he speaks very well.
“Para + infinitive” = “in order to”. It’s one of the most common structures in Spanish!
2. POR: where it comes from, where it passes through
Think of POR as something that comes FROM BEHIND (a cause) or PASSES THROUGH something.
I do it for (because of) my grandmother.
Pagué diez euros por el pan.
I paid ten euros for the bread.
“Gracias POR…” always with POR (the reason for the thanks): Gracias por tu ayuda, gracias por venir. Never “gracias para”!
Lo hago por ti. (because of you / on your behalf)
Lo hago para ti. (to give it to you)
Voy por pan. (I’m going to get bread)
Lo necesito para la mañana. (by the morning)
Why are you studying? — Because I like it. (the cause)
What are you studying for? — To work in Spain. (the purpose)
4. Set expressions with POR (learn them as they are)
And one with PARA, very common: “para siempre” (for ever).
Is it a purpose, a target, a recipient?
Is it a cause, a reason?
Don’t be discouraged: even advanced speakers make mistakes. The set expressions and “gracias por” / “para + infinitive” cover 80% of situations.

Tom bought a new bike with the lottery money. It was red, light and very fast. At last he could cycle to work.
Now he had a problem: what was he going to do with the old one? It had been sitting in the storeroom for years, covered in dust.
He thought about selling it online, but nobody would have paid much for it.
One Saturday, while he was walking around the neighbourhood, he saw a poster on the door of a charity: “We’re looking for bikes for young refugees.”
He went in out of curiosity. A volunteer explained that many young people needed bikes to get to school or work, because public transport was expensive for them.
The next day Tom took his old bike to the charity. But first he cleaned it, changed the tyres and fixed the brakes. He worked on it all morning.
There he met Ibrahim, a seventeen-year-old from Mali. He had arrived in Spain a year earlier, alone, by boat.
He spoke very good Spanish for the short time he had been here. He wanted to become a mechanic.
“This bike is for you,” Tom told him. Ibrahim looked at it with wide eyes. “For me? Why?”
“Because I don’t need it any more and you do. And because ten years ago, when I arrived in Madrid without knowing anyone, someone did something similar for me.”
Ibrahim thanked him for the bike and for fixing it. Then he asked: “Can you teach me to fix brakes? It’s for my mechanics exam.”
Since that day Tom has been going to the charity twice a week. In the afternoons they fix bikes together for other young people.
In June Ibrahim passed his exam with a nine. The first thing he did was call Tom.
“This mark is for you too,” he told him. Tom didn’t know what to say. For the first time in a long while, he felt truly useful.
Now there’s a new poster on the charity’s door, written by Ibrahim: “Free bike workshop. Tuesdays and Thursdays, from five to eight. For everyone”.
And underneath, in smaller letters: “Nobody arrives here alone”.
Tom reads it every time he goes in, and every time he thinks of that old, dusty bike.
¿Qué hizo Tom con la bicicleta vieja?
¿Cuántas veces por semana va Tom a la asociación?
